items.lbText:
Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem fell from ride earlier this month, spurring amusement park to temporarily shut it down

Six Flags will install seatbelts on its Goliath rollercoaster in Georgia , after a rider plummeted to his death earlier this month.

Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old father and educator, was thrown from his seat on the Goliath, a coaster that plunges riders down 165ft, before a second drop of 180ft. On his way down, he collided with the ride’s other cars.

Georgia authorities have launched a probe into Kariem’s death. The gruesome fall prompted the park to temporarily close the Goliath and eight rides at five other parks.

“What happened has deeply affected all of us at Six Flags. Safety has always been fundamental to the experience we provide for our guests,” the theme park’s CEO, John Reilly, wrote on Friday.

Seatbelts will also be added to coasters with a similar restraint, he announced, although an exact list remains unclear. The Goliath features a lap bar that locks over a rider’s waist, a design from Bolliger & Mabillard.

The park has also commissioned an independent review of the safety procedures for all of its attractions.

“I know trust is earned through actions and not words,” Reilly said. “We will continue to communicate about our progress and hold ourselves accountable to our commitments to you.”

The Six Flags Over Georgia fatal incident comes as the theme park is being sued over alleged bodily harm from its X2 ride at Magic Mountain. A recent CNN investigation uncovered a long history of brain injuries and at least two deaths linked to the ride.

A group of past riders who say they sustained brain injuries on X2 has accused the park of having a defective coaster and negligence for allowing its continued operation, according to court documents.

Six Flags permanently shut down the embattled X2 coaster in September.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of events in Europe – we will be closely following protests across the continent today.

In France , hundreds of thousands are expected at rallies across the country, with high school students, unionists, “yellow vest” demonstrators and others turning out for a fourth weekend of protests demanding more government funding for schools and measures to help with housing and the cost of living.

Desperate to avoid the looting and property damage seen on the fringes of some protests last weekend, French authorities have ramped up restrictions on where protesters can march and which groups are “authorised” to do so. They’ve increased policing 20%, mobilising 70,000 police officers and soldiers to the streets, including both elite units and trainee officers.

Many of Paris’s metro stations and major museums and tourist sites are shut today, while across the country, shops and businesses have been urged to close their doors. Community tensions are also high following a deadly shooting on Friday west of Paris where the gunman targeted non-white people, killing one person and injuring five others including a child. The French president called it a “racist terrorist attack”.

Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s anti-immigration party is also due to hold its national conference in the central city of Orléans. The far-right National Rally’s meeting is expected to draw up to 30,000 counter-demonstrators. Protests are also being held in Italy, Spain, Austria, Portugal, Albania and Ireland today.

items.lbText:
Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro

Tens of thousands of supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro .

Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%.

On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback . Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.

Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day.”

“The people have woken up,” Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have swept Brazil since the leftist’s first-round defeat, many led by students.

“Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again – and we don’t want dictatorship. We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career.

“There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes,” Silva claimed.

Polls suggest a far tighter margin and most analysts see Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, was president from 2019 to 2022 , as the slight favourite, having sold himself to voters as someone who will tackle chronic levels of violent crime with an iron fist.

However, in recent days Lula has appeared to regain the initiative and climb in the polls, amid a succession of scandals involving his rightwing foe. Last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of Brazil’s 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party attended by sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to strike a deal with the government of his father.

Some experts speculate a Lula comeback may be possible. At the Copacabana rally, activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “WE ARE GOING TO TURN THIS AROUND!”

“I’m super excited. Lula’s going to win,” said Marta Moraes, a 59-year-old restaurateur, as she joined Saturday’s demo.

Moraes said the election was not about left versus right. “We’ve nothing against the right … what we’re against is Bolsonarismo,” she said, tears filling her eyes as she recalled how Flávio Bolsonaro’s father botched the response to Covid during his chaotic 2019-2022 administration.

“I lost four members of my family because of Bolsonaro’s neglect,” Moraes said.

Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Many Brazilian democrats fear he will be released – and could even return to government – if his son wins. Reports in the Brazilian press suggest several of Bolsonaro’s fellow plotters – who are now in prison or hiding in exile – may be given top military and police jobs in a Bolsonaro administration.

Cammy Marinho, a 49-year-old DJ and activist, said: “I’m here to prevent democracy becoming extinct – which is what the Bolsonaro family wants”.

Marinho said she had spent the past fortnight fighting to persuade people who voted for Bolsonaro, or did not vote in the first round, to back Lula.

“It’s non-stop work: in the bakery, in the supermarket, on the underground – whenever you feel there is an opening to talk to someone and show to them the reality, everything that Lula has done and is doing for the people and everything that this [Bolsonaro] family has done against the people,” she said.

Many marchers were part of the so-called “Lula’s Army” – a 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was created after the first round in the hope of turning the election around.

“Being a soldier in Lula’s army … means fighting for Brazilian democracy. This isn’t a normal election,” said Isabella Gaze, 64, a retired teacher and one of the group’s members.

“They constantly claim Lula is corrupt. But the truth is that they represent the most rotten and worst part of Brazilian politics. This is what we are fighting against now,” Gaze said of the Bolsonaros.

Many of the faces on Copacabana beach were teenagers, including 14-year-old Heitor Lopes da Silva. Silva had come from the city of Duque de Caxias in his wheelchair, with a placard that said: “Lula, I’m a person with a disability and I’m here to support you.”

“My whole life I’ve believed Lula was a good president. [Bolsonaro] represents the destruction of Brazil …. he represents sadness and death,” he said of the Bolsonaro-era Covid catastrophe.

Large crowds of Bolsonaro supporters also hit the streets, including in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, which has Brazil’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo, and is a key bellwether. No presidential candidate has ever won the presidency without securing Minas Gerais, where Bolsonaro led by just under 5% in the first round.

Thousands of Bolsonaristas gathered to see their candidate in a palm-lined plaza called Praça da Liberdade. To the booming sound of AI-generated funk carioca tracks praising Bolsonaro, a sea of supporters dressed in Brazil’s yellow football jersey waved Brazilian flags – and many of the United States too.

“The US is a great nation. Who wouldn’t want to be aligned with them?” said 56-year-old cosmetics entrepreneur Marcos Antonio, holding a flag that merged the emblems of both countries.…

Anthony Lloyd forced his way out of a health unit in Lewisham, in south-east London, shortly after 4pm on Friday, the Metropolitan police said.

items.lbText:
Met police say Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen on Friday in south London, and ‘poses a risk to himself and the public’

A manhunt is under way to locate a prisoner who police say “poses a risk both to himself and the public” after he absconded from a medical facility in London .

Anthony Lloyd forced his way out of a health unit in Lewisham, in south-east London, shortly after 4pm on Friday, the Metropolitan police said.

The force warned the public not to approach Lloyd, but instead to contact 999 if he is spotted.

Lloyd was seen heading in the direction of Catford, police said in a statement on Saturday.

Lloyd was convicted in 2025 of actual bodily harm, according to the Press Association, relating to an incident in Nottinghamshire involving three emergency services workers.

He received a 12-month custodial sentence and was sent to prison . In September he was transferred to the medical facility in Lewisham.

The 38-year-old is white and about 5ft 8in, of medium build with short dark hair.

He was wearing a grey-blue T-shirt, black tracksuit bottoms and white trainers when last seen at about 4.10pm on Friday, police said.

Det supt Melanie Pressley, who is leading the manhunt, said: “We are conducting various significant inquiries to find Lloyd and return him to custody.

“We are concerned he poses a risk both to himself and the public, and would urge anyone who sees him to call 999 immediately. Do not approach him.

“If you have any information – however small – that could help us locate Lloyd, please get in touch with police as a matter of urgency.”

Officers believe Lloyd could be anywhere in the capital. He also has links to Surrey, Sussex, Thames Valley, Hampshire, Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire and Merseyside.

Anyone with information is asked to call 999, quoting the reference CAD4739/23Oct.

items.lbText:
Government estimates at least 400,000 people took part, but trade unions say the number is double that

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.

In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.

The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.

But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.

Police also fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police.

The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France . Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been almost 1,000 arrests.

More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years with public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country.

At Saturday’s protests, there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.

At the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.”

A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”

The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry.

At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in the gilets jaunes anti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from the gilets jaunes protest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue each weekend.

Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.”

Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them and we have to stand together.”

She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”

In Orléans, thousands of people shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress being held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration the National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, who is a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.

items.lbText:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy offers thanks to US allies for restoring system key to air defence and ‘frontline logistics’

Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government has said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted .

The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.

The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.

The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel , although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.

However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”

Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration , writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.

The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”

There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”

He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.

Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for ‌today is that Starlink ‌and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the ‌level we need.”

The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”

On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.

When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”

He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.

items.lbText:
Fender criticises stadium pricing, calling it ‘bollocks’ and says it ‘won’t be happening’ on his tour

Sam Fender has responded to criticism by fans about ticket prices for his 2027 stadium tour by promising he would lower the cost, telling followers on Instagram: “They’re getting changed.”

The 32-year-old musician announced his Proper Massive stadium tour earlier this week.

Gavin Davis, an Instagram user, shared details of standing tickets for Fender’s show at Wembley, which were split into “front standing”, costing £130.75, and “standing”, priced at £98.85. Prices for seating ranged between £64.75 and £130.75.

Responding to the post, Fender said he was “not happy with these prices”.

He said: “It got inflated well more than I’d had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on.”

In his reply, Fender also criticised the division of standing tickets into front and back tiers as “bollocks”, saying this “won’t be happening” on his tour.

“I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs,” he added.

Tickets at other venues were also listed at more than £100, with the highest ticket price in Newcastle at £112.90, in Cardiff £119, and in Edinburgh at £120.95. The top ticket price in Manchester was £119.60.

Tickets for the tour are due to go on sale on Friday, with a presale on Wednesday morning.

Fender is not the first pop star to criticise ticket prices for his own show. The Swedish pop singer Zara Larsson has also called out steep ticket prices. In a TikTok post in August, she agreed with criticism from fans that ticket prices for her show in Bangkok were “very expensive” and wished to be “more involved” with setting prices.

“I hate the fact that people genuinely want to come, but they can’t because of the prices,” Larsson added.

Fender will perform at Newcastle’s St James’s Park, Cardiff’s Principality Stadium, Dublin’s Marley Park, Murrayfield in Edinburgh and the Etihad in Manchester across summer 2027.

Earlier this week, Fender also confirmed there would be a fourth album but he has yet to release the title or cover.

Fender, who was born in North Shields in Tyne and Wear, is best-known for his hit songs Hypersonic Missiles, Seventeen Going Under and People Watching. He is also the winner of five Brit awards and received the Mercury prize for his 2025 album People Watching.

Earlier this year, Fender rerecorded his single Rein Me In as a duet with the English singer-songwriter Olivia Dean, which won 2026 song of the year at the Brit awards. The song spent 23 overall weeks at No 1 in the singles chart, making it the longest-running No 1 single in British history.

items.lbText:
Fund will support feasibility study for potential bid to host Games in 2040s, backed by northern mayors and top athletes

John Healey is to announce a £7m fund to examine a potential future bid to host the Olympics in northern England in his first budget as chancellor.

The fund will be used to carry out a full feasibility study for a northern Games, which, if successful, would be held in the north of England in the 2040s.

In May, before Andy Burnham entered No 10, the government commissioned an assessment by UK Sport which could inform a bid for the international sporting event in the 2040s. If the campaign were successful, it would be the first time the Olympic Games and Paralympics were hosted in Britain since London 2012.

There was further momentum behind the idea in June when mayors from across the north of England met in Sheffield to discuss the possibility of a northern Olympic bid.

More than 40 Olympians, Paralympians and elite athletes, including Laura Kenny, Jason Kenny, Sarah Storey, Beth Tweddle and Tom Pidcock, have signed a joint statement “to express our strong and united support” for the idea to hold a “box office Games” in the north of England.

Announcing the fund, Burnham said an Olympics bid would “unlock opportunity across our towns and cities” and that “we can put on the greatest show on Earth”.

He continued: “Few things bring a country together quite like the Olympics. I want people to feel that sense of excitement again, and to experience it in their own towns and communities, not just watch it on the telly.

“The Games would unlock opportunity across our towns and cities for the whole country. From north to south, it would be something everyone could get behind and be proud of.

“We know we can put on the greatest show on earth. Now we want to explore how we can do it again, with the whole country behind it.”

The full feasibility study will look in greater detail at how the Games would work in practice, including types of venues and transport links needed and the prospects of developing a winning bid. It will also look into how much it could cost and examine the chances of a bid succeeding.

The work will involve the government, UK Sport, the northern mayors and the British Olympic and Paralympic Associations, who would ultimately be responsible for a bid.

Healey said: “The north hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable.

“Britain’s experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I’m picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious Games.

“It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost.”

The British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport released a joint statement welcoming the news.

“Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements,” they said.

Sydney, Tokyo and London are among the mega-cities that have played host to the Olympics in recent years but Brisbane, Australia’s third-largest city, will be hosting the 2032 Games.

The Mayor of London Sadiq Khan has previously criticised plans to explore a bid to host the Olympics in northern England, saying that excluding London would be a “missed opportunity”.

items.title: Suspect arrested over fire at Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ retreat in Bavaria
items.author: Donna Ferguson and agencies
items.content:
About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle blaze at former Nazi mountain retreat in remote part of southern Germany

Police have arrested a 33-year-old German citizen after a fire ripped through Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat in Bavaria, leaving the historic Nazi meeting place – known as the Eagle’s Nest – largely destroyed.

About 200 firefighters were deployed on Friday night to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote, purpose-built Kehlsteinhaus residence, a protected building on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle the blaze at former Nazi retreat in a remote part of southern Germany

German police said Saturday they had detained a suspect after a fire at Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat, known as the Eagle’s Nest, in the state of Bavaria.

About 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote and difficult-to-access Kehlsteinhaus residence, on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany .

Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said.

“A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody,” they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the blaze.

Police spokesperson Lisa Maier said firefighters struggled to tackle the fire due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000 feet).

The building was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.

Authorities were alerted to the fire on Friday evening, when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.50pm (1950 GMT), police said.

No potential reason for the fire was given, but the German media reported that the investigators suspected it was the result of arson.

As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle’s Nest was still engulfed in flames in the early hours of Saturday, a weather camera showed.

Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an AFP photographer.

The firefighters found no one inside the building.

Maier said police were still investigating but will hold a news conference later on Saturday.

German tabloid Bild reported that the authorities had arrested a motorcyclist they came across on their way to the scene.

Built between 1937 and 1938, the Eagle’s Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and Communists in the Holocaust.

It was designed to serve as a monument to Hitler’s rule, although the dictator rarely visited the complex.

It survived the second world war undamaged, and since 1952 has hosted an exhibition recounting the house’s Nazi history and a restaurant.

items.title: Nine killed and 40 injured after gunmen open fire at church funeral in Jordan
items.author: Reuters in Al-Mushairfeh
items.content:
Footage broadcast on state TV shows three attackers approaching Greek Orthodox church and firing shots

Nine people have been killed after gunmen opened fire at a funeral at a church in Jordan in a rare attack ⁠on the country’s Christian minority.

Authorities described the attack on Friday as a terrorist act by extremists.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Footage broadcast on state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.

The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 180km (110 miles) south of the capital, Amman.

Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church.

Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church.

Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. “It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire,” Halasa said.

He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan’s security services did not immediately release details.

A government statement said that the attack was “carried out by unknown assailants,” but didn’t say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that “investigations are under way at full speed”.

Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom’s Petra news agency.

Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff.

Jordan’s health minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition.

King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan “will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties” and offered his “deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded”.

Jordan’s prime minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism.

Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman.

Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world’s foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday’s shooting, calling it a “heinous terrorist attack.”

Iraqi foreign minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and “affirmed Iraq’s solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism”, Hussein’s office said in a statement.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as “especially heinous,” spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said. “The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account.”

items.lbText:
Scotland Yard says it shared letter about Thomas Markle Sr allegations in 2019 but did not pass claims to other agencies

The Metropolitan police have confirmed they gave a letter to the Duchess of Sussex in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, after accusations arose on Friday about Thomas Markle Sr having child sexual abuse images.

Scotland Yard said it had received a letter in January 2019 making a number of allegations about offending outside Britain.

The police force said it had passed the information on to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s office, but it did not pass it on to “other law enforcement agencies”.

The Sun newspaper published claims that Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, claimed he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.

On Friday, Meghan said she had been made aware of these allegations by the Met, and that she was “deeply distressed” by them.

The duchess, who is estranged from her father said in a statement she had broken off contact to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them.

Meghan and Prince Harry recently moved back to the UK from the US.

Meghan’s father has denied the allegations and told the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”.

The Met said it was considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions.

In a statement, a Metropolitan police spokesperson said: “Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS (Metropolitan Police Service) Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.

“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”

In a statement on Friday, issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”

She later said she had misremembered the year the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.

A spokesperson for the Duchess of Sussex said: “In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months.

“If the MPS holds a time-stamped record confirming that the letter was reviewed in 2019, that should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the duchess.

“I think it is reasonable to recognise that she is doing her best to recall the precise timing of events that were not diarised at the time, and that any discrepancy of a few months is an understandable consequence of that passage of time.”

Sources said that although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.

The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.

Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.

items.title: Kim Jong-un crosses newly opened bridge into China
items.author: Raphael Rashid in Seoul
items.content:
North Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party member

Kim Jong-un has visited China, inaugurating a bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hopes to expand cooperation with his neighbour.

The North Korean leader arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday after crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, according to South Korea’s unification ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua news agency.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
North Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party member

Kim Jong-un has visited China, inaugurating a bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hopes to expand cooperation with his neighbour.

The North Korean leader arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday after crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, according to South Korea’s unification ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua news agency.

He met Wang Huning, a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party. The pair toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship.

Kim said his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries”, according to Xinhua.

Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, Xinhua said.

The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of Kim’s ties with Beijing ahead of the 25 October anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean war, which came days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950.

Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum about China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.

Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.

The 3km bridge opened in mid-October , 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border, leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.

The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June , his first trip there in seven years.

Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.

Xi will host the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.

Reuters reported on Friday , however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.

Associated Press contributed to this report

items.title: Storm Boelo to bring 80mph gusts and heavy rain to parts of UK
items.author: Priya Bharadia
items.content:
Second named storm will hit northern parts of UK as thousands remain without power after Friday’s Storm Austen

The UK is bracing for a second storm this weekend, as strong winds and heavy rain are expected to disrupt travel and cause further power cuts in the north.

Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, is expected to bring heavy, frequent showers and winds potentially exceeding 80mph to northern parts of the UK.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Second named storm in as many days will hit northern parts of UK as thousands remain without power after Friday’s Storm Austen

The UK is bracing for a second storm this weekend, as strong winds and heavy rain are expected to disrupt travel and cause further power cuts in the north.

Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, is expected to bring heavy, frequent showers and winds potentially exceeding 80mph to northern parts of the UK.

Thousands of homes in the south-west of England have already been left without power after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday.

The Met Office has advised people to stay indoors as much as possible, and said the storm will bring danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.

The forecaster has issued an amber alert, its second most severe weather warning, covering Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm Saturday to the same time on Sunday. Another amber warning is also in place for the north-east of Northern Ireland from 9pm Saturday to 10am Sunday.

A large yellow warning for very wet and windy weather will cover the whole of the UK’s north from midday Saturday to 9pm on Sunday. Another warning for heavy rain covers Wales and parts of western and southern England from 11am to 11pm Saturday.

Widespread travel disruption is expected on ferries and trains. TransPennine Express has warned against making all but essential train journeys on Saturday and Sunday, while Avanti West Coast has strongly advised users not to travel north of Preston on Sunday.

The Met Office has also warned that power cuts across the south-west of England could be replicated across amber areas in the north this weekend.

In the south-west of England, 31,000 homes were without power at one stage on Friday. More than 3,700 were still without electricity on Saturday morning, according to the National Grid map.

Human-driven climate change has continued to reshape rainfall patterns and weather conditions globally. The UK experienced its hottest summer on record this year, with five heatwaves and a record-breaking 40 days of temperatures above 30C.

Met Office meteorologist Alex Burkill said: “Storm Boelo is arriving. It’s going to bring widespread rain and some very strong winds indeed, and it’s quick on the tails of Storm Austen which is now clearing away towards the east.

“It’s the winds that were perhaps most concerned about, they’re really going to whip up some strong gusty winds across Northern Ireland, northern parts of England and also Scotland through the day – strengthening as we head towards the evening.

“Temperatures will be a little more than the seasonal average but “obviously with the wind and rain it’s going to feel pretty unpleasant out there,” Burkhill added. “A very, well, different side of autumn compared with what we’ve seen through much of the season so far.”

Storm Boelo’s winds are expected to peak from Saturday evening. The wet weather will clear overnight in many areas, while more rain continues to hit Scotland and northern Ireland.

Attending a summit on the summer’s record wildfires on Friday, Andy Burnham warned that the UK could face “a winter of greater flooding” .

The prime minister denied suggestions that the government was playing catch-up with civil preparedness, but said “we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common”.

items.lbText:
PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint

Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families, in collective punishment for a militant attack on an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.

The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.

Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.

People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.

The large-scale demolitions follow an attack on Friday on an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20 minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.

The attack came four days before Israeli elections, and the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu , and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.

Netanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.

Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.

A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.

A Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”

Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.

“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”

The Israeli army was approached for comment on the operations and on videos showing extensive devastation.

The new data reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) comes as experts criticize the agency for lack of transparency, and as health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr takes steps to further upend US vaccine infrastructure.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 4,588 cases across the country, more than double the tally in 2025

Federal health authorities reported an additional 178 cases of measles in the US this week, as the vaccine-preventable illness continues to sicken people across at least 43 outbreaks.

The new data reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) comes as experts criticize the agency for lack of transparency, and as health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr takes steps to further upend US vaccine infrastructure.

The CDC reported 4,588 cases of measles across the country in 2026 as of Friday – more than double the tally for 2025. Pennsylvania alone reported 1,338 cases on the same day. The CDC also reported large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah, both of which are reporting more than 500 cases.

In spite of rising measles numbers, official tallies represent an undercount of the disease. Measles is widely regarded as one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine. Its most common symptoms – rash, runny nose, fever and cough – may not immediately send the infected to a doctor.

Measles sends one in five unvaccinated people who become infected to the hospital, and one to three people in 1,000 die of disease-related complications. The measles vaccine is 97% effective at preventing the disease. Vaccine side effects include injection-site soreness and low-grade fever. The measles vaccine has been a focal point of anti-vaccine activism for decades.

In Pennsylvania, which has had the worst outbreak in the nation for months, state authorities have reported five measles-associated deaths and are investigating a sixth. The CDC has reported three measles deaths nationally, but has refused to say where the third death took place, obscuring whether it is counting a death in Pennsylvania or elsewhere.

Kennedy reportedly asked senior CDC officials in September to remove a measles death from the official tally after he questioned whether the disease contributed to the death, according to Reuters .

In addition to criticism of how the CDC has tallied measles deaths, Health and Human Services (HHS) this week announced changes to vaccine injury reporting systems. A proposal will allow doctors to bill for reporting suspected vaccine injuries, among other changes.

The “vaccine adverse event reporting system”, or VAERS, has been a long-time fixation of the anti-vaccine movement. The system has proved useful for researchers tracking rare vaccine safety issues. However, it has also become a source of misinformation for anti-vaccine activists, who point to VAERS to make claims, however unfounded, about safety.

All vaccines have risks – a fact acknowledged by vaccinologists . Before Kennedy’s appointment to the health department, an expert panel considered each vaccine change individually to decide whether benefits outweigh risks. Kennedy fired all 17 sitting members of that board. He replaced them with members with whom he ideologically aligned. A court blocked the members’ appointment in March.

In his time as secretary, Kennedy also misleadingly claimed children get more than 90 vaccine doses ; linked vaccines to autism in spite of extensive evidence to the contrary; directed the CDC to remove claims that vaccines do not cause autism from its website; claimed the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine contains “ aborted fetal debris ”; and stated that vitamin A and cod liver oil may help children with measles, which leading physicians described as misleading.

items.lbText:
Other voter concerns have prevailed but return of Congress likely to see renewed focus on late sex offender’s activities

As US voters head to the polls for crucial and fraught midterm elections, some survivors’ advocates in the Jeffrey Epstein investigation have expressed concern that the scandal could recede into the background.

Political experts believe, however, the Epstein issue is not going away permanently and that many voters can balance day-to-day concerns such as affordability and AI with the scandal involving the late financier and accused sex trafficker whose social circle was widespread among America’s elite.

“My greatest concern is not that the public will forget Jeffrey Epstein, but that the politicians and institutions responsible for accountability will use the chaos of world events as an excuse to move on,” said Spencer Kuvin of Goldlaw, who has represented multiple Epstein survivors.

Kuvin added: “Wars, economic crises and political controversies may dominate the headlines, but they do not erase the suffering of the victims or the unanswered questions about how Epstein and his powerful associates were allowed to operate for decades.

“Justice should not have an expiration date, and it certainly should not be dictated by the news cycle. We cannot allow the Epstein scandal to become yesterday’s news simply because today’s headlines are more urgent.”

Kuvin called for the US government to continue releasing Epstein files – which many have said were excluded from allegedly incomplete disclosures – and for Congress to demand accountability.

“It has been disappointing to have seen attention diverted from Jeffrey Epstein in the past year,” said Jennifer Freeman of Marsh Law, who represents numerous Epstein survivors in litigation surrounding his sexual abuse of teenage girls.

Freeman, however, expressed optimism about the long-term prospects of justice for survivors, saying: “While public attention may have shifted from the Epstein case, given the electoral cycle, I am confident it will command concentration and accountability shortly again.”

Freeman noted that she was continuing to pursue a lawsuit against the US government for alleged negligence “in repeatedly, for decades, dropping the ball on investigating and prosecuting Epstein”. She is also litigating a class-action lawsuit against his estate related to his collection and production of child sex abuse images.

Political experts said that Epstein might get less attention from campaigning politicians and voters, but that it was probably a temporary dip, not a permanent drop-off.

“It really does feel like everything is on fire. I think people can care about several things at once, but what’s directly affecting their lives tends to take priority,” Brittany Martinez, a Republican strategist who works as acting director of Principles First, said. “When they’re worried about gas prices, living costs and whether their government is working for them, that can push Epstein out of the immediate conversation.

“I don’t think the questions or the demand for answers have gone away; they’re just competing for attention. So I’d expect to hear less about it for stretches, rather than see it disappear altogether.”

“There’s just something every day with Trump,” said Shawn Donahue, clinical associate professor in the University at Buffalo’s department of political science.

For Donahue, timing also plays a key role. The US Congress has been in recess and without members on the House floor, so there’s not any discussion of the Epstein Files Transparency Act’s proposed new iteration. This bill, the Epstein Files Transparency Act II , seeks to address what advocates have said are shortfalls in the present EFTA – such as an absence of enforcement mechanisms.

“It kind of feels like whenever Congress comes back into session, this probably starts to become more of an issue again, and especially if Democrats are looking at being in control of one or maybe both chambers of Congress,” Donahue said.

Should Democrats win the house, as polls project, Donahue expects they will swiftly “put Republicans on the spot” with Epstein. “Democrats are ready to start on the investigation from day one.”

For Julie Roginsky, who co-founded the non-profit Lift Our Voices and pursued a sexual harassment lawsuit against the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes, the significance of Epstein among voters has not gone away.

“I think Epstein is part of the reason that Trump’s numbers are at record lows . I think it’s something that was one of the issues where even Maga Republicans broke with him,” Roginsky said. “I think that if Democrats do get control of at least one house of Congress this year, then starting next year, you’re going to see a lot more conversation about survivors and about Epstein.”

Congressional supporters of survivors said they would keep fighting for truth and justice.

“This is bigger than a moment. It’s a reckoning, and Americans are ready to have this conversation about power, abuse, and who gets protected,” the Democratic New Mexico representative Teresa Leger Fernández said in a statement. “Of course, Americans will vote with their pocketbooks. They’re worried about groceries, gas, and making rent. But they won’t forget that this president was Epstein’s friend and tried to hide the truth from them.

“The survivors have fought for decades to be heard. Our responsibility is to keep fighting alongside them, get the truth out, and hold those responsible accountable. That responsibility doesn’t disappear when the headlines change.”

The Massachusetts Democratic representative Ayanna Pressley said in a statement: “Justice for survivors of Epstein’s abuse has been a prominent issue amongst the electorate because people of conscience see through the cover-ups of the Trump Administration and demand accountability – that won’t change no matter how much they try to flood the zone and distract us.”…

items.lbText:
Nazhat Shameem Khan claims some staff are facing ‘banking difficulties’ but their work is unaffected

The deputy prosecutor of the international criminal court has said new US sanctions are beginning to take effect on its staff but insisted they have not hindered the court’s work.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, announced the sanctions this month , accusing the ICC – a frequent target of the Trump administration – of being a “rogue court” and declaring: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”

Nazhat Shameem Khan, who is co-running the office pending the appointment of a new chief prosecutor, said the court was so far continuing its work.

She said the Gaza war investigation and others had made “significant progress” since war crimes arrest warrants were issued in November 2024 for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister, Yoav Galant. Further applications from the prosecutor were being kept secret by order of the court, she said.

Some ICC staff had however encountered banking problems, she said, even though the US sanctions on the court were not due to take effect until six months from 9 October, the date of their announcement. She said the banks were “over-complying” to minimise risk while there was uncertainty over the ultimate scope of the measures.

“These are sanctions imposed on the institutions and, in principle, our individual members should not be impacted directly,” the Fijian deputy prosecutor said in an interview with the Guardian. “But again, what I am hearing from members of our staff is that some of them are experiencing difficulties in banking.”

The court is working on insulating itself from sanctions imposed by a hostile administration in Washington. It has switched its software from Microsoft to European ​alternatives, and is negotiating with relevant service providers over banking and health insurance.

“All the investigations across all situations continue. We haven’t made any decision based on the sanctions to reduce our capability or reduce our output,” Khan said, acknowledging that it was impossible to anticipate the full impact of sanctions when they officially took effect.

The new sanctions target the whole institution of the ICC, but the US first targeted 13 ICC staff in February 2025. Khan was one of them, so is accustomed to dealing with sanctions, which affect aspects of everyday life.

“Life without a credit card is inconvenient. It’s amazing how many things now we cannot do around the world, particularly in relation to travel, without a credit card,” she said, but added that her inconvenience was put into perspective when she visited refugee camps or sites of mass atrocities.

“We see the faces of our victims for whom sanctions and credit cards are completely irrelevant. They just want justice.”

American sanctions are not the only disruption to the ICC prosecutors’ work. Formal investigations began in late November 2024 into allegations of sexual harassment against the former chief prosecutor, Karim Khan. The British jurist (who is no relation to the deputy prosecutor) denied the charges. He was removed in July this year after a vote by member states.

No further charges over the Gaza war have been announced since late 2024. Khan insisted that investigative work on the Israel-Palestine file had only gone quiet because of the court’s ruling earlier this year that all charges and applications for warrants should be kept secret until the judges decide they can be made public.

“Even if we reach a stage of the investigations where it might be imminent, we may not discuss it publicly,” she said. “And so while there might be an appearance that nothing is happening, I can assure you that there’s significant progress in that particular situation as well as others.”

When announcing the sanctions, Rubio gave the ICC a six-month grace period “to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns” but it is unclear what would satisfy the Trump administration , which has exhibited a longstanding hostility towards the court.

Rubio claimed, without evidence, this month that “globalist ‘experts’ an ocean away” wanted the ICC to prosecute US citizens. Khan said it was unclear who and what Rubio had in mind.

“It is possible that there is a mistaken belief on the part of those who are concerned that we are pursuing Americans, but we certainly haven’t brought any Americans before the court,” she said. “If his reference is to Afghanistan, then in fact the priority for the investigation is in relation to offences committed specifically against women, girls and other vulnerable groups by the Taliban and by the Islamic State Khorasan in Afghanistan.”

This month, four arrest warrants were unsealed by the ICC pretrial chamber against members of the Taliban on charges of gender persecution.

The court registrar for the ICC is in negotiation with the EU over blocking the US sanctions or protecting the court in other ways. There has been support for the court, and on Thursday, the European parliament awarded its Sakharov prize for freedom of thought to the court and its officials.

Khan said the support was “a very important message that the staff at the court need to hear”, as were pledges from other countries to continue to contribute towards the ICC’s costs.

“I think that the fact that there is so much attention on us is a reflection of how relevant we are,” Khan said. “This is a court that provides an avenue of justice for victims who have nowhere else to go, who really want to cut past politics and want their voices to be heard.”

items.title: New Trump rule allows hunters to bait bears in Alaska with doughnuts, bacon and more
items.author: Tom Perkins

Critics decry Trump administration rule that lets hunters lure bears with human foods on federal lands in Alaska

A new Trump administration rule allows hunters to bait bears on federal lands in Alaska with bacon, doughnuts, meat scraps or other human foods typically used to help kill the trophy animals at close range.

Opponents say the practice will cause bears to be more aggressive around humans, and allege that the rule change is a political gift to largely rightwing trophy hunters. The rule replaces a 2024 Biden administration rule that banned the practice, and environmental groups criticized the move as “indefensible and inexcusable”.

“We are discouraged to see this rule come back, specifically the bear baiting piece which is cruel and dangerous, not only to wildlife but the public as well,” said Drew Robertson, senior regulatory specialist for Humane World for Animals .

The US interior department on Friday published the rule on the federal register, and it will take effect in mid-November. It marks the latest in a series of rule changes at the state and federal levels since 2023 that allow trophy hunters to use what critics say are barbaric and unethical practices to kill animals.

Doug Burgum, the secretary of the interior, wrote in a press release that the latest rule was developed in response to demands by Alaska residents and it was a “commonsense framework and gives Alaskans a stronger voice in decisions affecting the lands, wildlife and traditions they know best”.

The federal rule does not list specific foods that are allowed, but it defers to state rules, which allow for baiting, and hunters typically use “the cheapest and most effective food, which is high fat and high sugar”, said Nicholas Arrivo, a managing attorney at Animal Protection Law. Hunters typically put food in a steel drum or garbage can, monitor the bait, then set up from a nearby blind from which they kill the bear at short range, Arrivo said.

The practice raises broader ethical questions around the spirit and intent of sport hunting.

“It is a more extreme practice than the hunting traditions that people think of, and many hunters would not see this as a fair chase,” Robertson said.

The move comes after Alaska and federal officials in recent years started allowing sport hunters to hunt big game with controversial practices, like shooting bears from helicopters, shooting swimming caribou from motor boats, killing wolf pups in their dens and using artificial lights to draw bears out of the dens to kill them. The bear baiting is not highly unusual as about a dozen states allow similar practices, but more do not.

The rule change came at the direction of Donald Trump in an executive order , called Unleashing Alaska’s Extraordinary Resource Potential, which was issued in his second administration’s early days.

“It was a priority for the president … and he included direction to reissue this rule, which says that there is a political motivation, not something that seems to be derived from careful consideration,” Robertson said.

This baiting rule has a long history. A ban was first put in place by Barack Obama’s administration, then undone by the first Trump administration. Litigation upheld the Obama rule and overturned the Trump rule. The Biden administration then reimplemented the rule in 2024, largely because science shows that the practice will make bears more aggressive, and put park visitors’ lives at risk.

Though the Trump administration has said the rule was designed to give the state more control over the land, the lands are federal and Congress created the federal land program to give the federal government decision-making power, not state governments, Arrivo said. He said it “is anathema to federal land management goals … of preserving wildlife diversity”.

Though no decision has yet been made about a lawsuit, Arrivo said the interior department’s decision to fully scrap the 2024 rule that underwent a more robust scientific process “doesn’t smell right and raises questions about the legality of this rule”.

Leading restaurateur says Gulf countries actively help businesses set up, while east Asia has a better work ethic

Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur.

James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf.

Other restaurants have opened in Dubai , including the celebrity hotspot Scott’s in Mayfair, the two Michelin-starred Indian venue Gymkhana, and the upmarket Chinese restaurant Park Chinois. Isabel’s, a Mayfair institution enjoyed by politicians, has opened in Abu Dhabi. And the trendy Borough Market bakery Bread Ahead has branched out in Dubai.

Despite conflicts in the Middle East, including the US-Israeli war in Iran which caused Dubai to face bombardment and an exodus of expats earlier this year, restaurants continue to open in the emirate.

Speaking from Hong Kong, where he is looking at opportunities in Asia, Robson said: “East Asia, the States and the Gulf are key growth targets for us. America champions business, the Gulf actively encourages and assists, whilst east Asia has a work ethic and taxation system that puts the UK to shame. I’m incredibly keen to start working in these regions over the next few years.”

Fallow has risen to fame partially through Instagram, where it has 650,000 followers, and its striking dishes including a whole cod’s head drenched in a spicy butter sauce.

Restaurateurs have complained of the VAT rate for hospitality in the UK, which at 20% is one of the highest rates in Europe. The European average for restaurants is about 12%. In Italy, it is set at 10% for food sold in restaurants. Chefs are calling for Andy Burnham to use next week’s budget to cut the VAT rate.

“We have had a tsunami of taxes that have got to the point where taking business risk simply does not make sense in the UK,” Robson said, “Sadly the country has sleepwalked into multiple anti-growth taxations the last two budgets and likely more will be forthcoming next week.”

The entrepreneur has asked for VAT to be put more in line with Europe. “Add 25% corporation tax and 40%-plus dividend tax, then you start to question why do businesses any more.”

Jason Atherton, a Michelin-starred chef, spends a third of his time at his Dubai restaurant now and says it is easier to make a profit abroad than in London.

But human rights experts have warned of exploitation and poor worker protections in the Gulf. Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s director of campaigns, said: “Dubai might look like an attractive place to do business, but the UAE has a very poor record on workers’ rights and protection from labour exploitation. The UAE has spent heavily on polishing its image in the UK, not least through Manchester City, but that glamour shouldn’t distract from how the people who keep its economy running are treated.

“Migrant workers, who make up the majority of the UAE’s population, remain bound by a sponsorship system that ties them to their employers and exposes them to labour abuse. They are denied the right to form trade unions, leaving them few ways to challenge unfair treatment.

“Any UK business expanding into the Gulf has a responsibility to carry out proper human rights due diligence, to make sure the people working in its kitchens are treated fairly, paid properly and able to raise concerns without fear of losing their job or visa.”

Some restaurants in Dubai are struggling: Dinner by Heston is temporarily closed and has been since the fallout from the war in the Middle East. The Michelin guide came under fire earlier this month because it included 16 restaurants that were either permanently or temporarily closed. It appears that some visits were undertaken by inspectors at the beginning of the year, before the war started.

Robson said he had no resentment paying UK tax. “I am incredibly proud of the taxes I pay and feel privileged that I can contribute to our country’s deficit and will continue to do so,” he said. “My point is UK growth simply does not have any risk-reward balance any more, therefore it’s play incredibly safe here and focus overseas.”

items.lbText:
Mother, 36, died after current off North Bimini reportedly swept away two boys, who were later rescued, police say

A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling.

The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday.

The force said they believed she was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island of North Bimini when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.

The police said that in an attempt to rescue her boys, “the woman was also swept away”. The children were later rescued from the water.

The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support.

Bimini is a small island group between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland.

The islands are best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and are also home to a world-leading shark research centre.

In a statementposted on social media, the Royal Bahamas police force said: “According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini ferry dock.

“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.

“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.

“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.

“She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. Foul play is not suspected at this time.”

An autopsy would be carried out to help determine the exact cause of death, the statement said.

A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.

“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”

Founding member of Planxty, Lunny went on to play for bands such as Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin

The Irish traditional musician Dónal Lunny has died at the age of 79 from cancer.

Lunny rose to prominence in the trio Rakes of Kildare alongside his brother Frank and Christy Moore. He went on to play in bands such as Planxty , Moving Hearts , the Bothy Band and Coolfin among others and toured the world.

A post on his Facebook page confirmed that Lunny died in St James’s hospital in Dublin on Friday morning.

“We are heartbroken to confirm that our beloved Dónal passed away peacefully this morning in Dublin following a short stay in St James’s hospital,” the post said. “Thank you for helping us to remember and celebrate his immense contribution to music, to culture and to so many people’s lives all over the world.”

The Irish president, Catherine Connolly, expressed her “deepest condolences to the family, friends and many musical collaborators of Dónal Lunny”.

In a statement, she said: “Dónal was one of Ireland’s greatest musical figures, a wonderfully talented musician and producer who was central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music.

“Dónal will be particularly remembered for his long partnerships with fellow musicians such as Christy Moore and Andy Irvine and for the innovative music he has left behind both as a musician in groups including Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts and also as a renowned producer.

“This rich musical legacy, including his central role in the introduction of the bouzouki into Irish music, was appropriately recognised by his fellow artists in Dónal’s membership of Aosdána, as well as the well-deserved recognition which he received in being awarded a lifetime achievement award at the 2025 RTÉ Radio 1 Irish folk awards.

“Beyond his music, Dónal will be remembered for his warmth and the strong connection which he had with audiences all over Ireland and beyond. He will be deeply missed.”

The post ended in Irish, saying his likes will not be seen again: “ Ní bheidh a leithéid arís ann .”

Lunny was born in Tullamore, County Offaly, and was a multi-instrumentalist but was best known for his mastery of the bouzouki. He was a talented melody writer and considered central to the revival of traditional music as he produced 17 albums under his record label Mulligan Records.

The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he was “deeply saddened” to hear of Lunny’s death. “A colossus of Irish music, as a performer, songwriter and producer,” he wrote in a post on social media.

“Uniquely gifted, Dónal carried traditional and folk music to new audiences through Planxty and his many other endeavours.”

Sinn Féin’s president, Mary Lou McDonald, also paid tribute online, saying: “Deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Dónal Lunny. A giant of Irish traditional music, Dónal helped shape the sound of Irish music for generations, bringing our rich musical heritage to audiences at home and around the world. His contribution to Irish music and culture will never be forgotten.

“ Ar dheis Dé go raibh a anam [May his soul rest in peace].”
